qs.q: During the therapeutic drainage of a suspected amoebic liver abscess, what distinctive macroscopic appearance is classically expected of the aspirated necrotic material?
o: Anchovy paste-like reddish-brown thick liquid
Bright green purulent fluid with foul odor
Clear serous exudate with occasional blood flecks
Bright yellow creamy pus with high viscosity
Dark black tarry fluid containing digested blood
qs.e: Amebic liver abscess aspiration yields characteristic chocolate-brown or anchovy paste-like necrotic material lacking neutrophils.
qs.s: Weekly Year 2: Parasitology Exam - October 30, 2026 (Section A: MCQs)

qs.q: When is therapeutic needle aspiration specifically indicated in the management of a suspected amoebic liver abscess?
o: To differentiate amoebic from pyogenic pus
When no response to therapy occurs in days
To prevent the development of effusion
As a routine first-line diagnostic procedure
qs.e: Aspiration is not conventionally required unless there is no response to therapy after 3-5 days or the abscess is at immediate risk of rupture. Routine aspiration is discouraged because medical therapy is highly effective.

qs.q: What is the characteristic macroscopic appearance of the fluid obtained from an aspirated amoebic liver abscess?
o: Bright red bloody hemorrhagic fluid
Foul-smelling purulent green pus fluid
Chocolate-colored anchovy paste fluid
Clear straw-colored transudative fluid
qs.e: The aspirate consists of an acellular proteinaceous debris described as chocolate-colored anchovy paste fluid. Purulent green pus is more typical of pyogenic bacterial abscesses.

qs.q: A patient presents with a suspected amoebic liver abscess. Which of the following laboratory findings is typically present in the peripheral blood?
o: Isolated thrombocytopenia
Pancytopenia presentation
Leucocytosis without eosinophilia
Marked eosinophilia present
qs.e: Peripheral blood testing in hepatic amoebiasis typically demonstrates leucocytosis without eosinophilia. Eosinophilia is characteristic of helminthic infections rather than amoebic liver abscesses.

qs.q: What is the appearance of the classic fluid aspirated from an amoebic liver abscess?
o: Chocolate colored anchovy paste
Bright red hemorrhagic blood
Foul-smelling green pus
Clear serous fluid aspirate
qs.e: The aspirate of an amoebic liver abscess typically consists of an acellular proteinaceous debris described as a chocolate-colored anchovy paste fluid. Foul-smelling green pus is more characteristic of pyogenic bacterial abscesses.

qs.q: When is therapeutic aspiration specifically indicated in the management of an amoebic liver abscess?
o: As a routine first-line procedure for all patients
When there is no response to medical therapy after 3-5 days
Whenever trophozoites are seen in routine stool microscopy
To definitively rule out primary pyogenic infection prior to treatment
qs.e: Aspiration is not routinely required but is specifically considered when there is no response to medical therapy after 3-5 days or if the abscess is at immediate risk of rupture. Routine first-line aspiration is generally not recommended.

qs.q: When is therapeutic or diagnostic aspiration conventionally recommended in the management of an amoebic liver abscess?
o: When small bowel absorption impairs oral intake.
When therapy fails after 3-5 days.
As a mandatory first-line procedure for all patients.
Routinely to confirm diagnosis in uncomplicated cases.
qs.e: Aspiration is not routinely required unless there is no response to therapy after 3-5 days or the abscess is at immediate risk of rupture. It enhances clinical recovery in cases refractory to medical treatment.

qs.q: What is the characteristic macroscopic appearance of fluid aspirated from an amoebic liver abscess?
o: Bright yellow fluid rich in biliary pigments.
Clear serous fluid with high protein.
Purulent green fluid with many neutrophils.
Chocolate-colored anchovy-paste fluid.
qs.e: The aspirate typically consists of a chocolate colored 'Anchovy Paste' fluid representing acellular proteinaceous debris and necrotic hepatocytes. Trophozoites are rarely seen on microscopy in the fluid.

ai.title: Amoebic Liver Abscess

ai.summary: A parasitic infection of the liver by Entamoeba histolytica presenting with RUQ pain, fever and a hypoechoic lesion. Diagnosis relies on imaging, serology and aspirate microscopy. Treatment is metronidazole plus supportive care.

sections.p: A focal collection of necrotic tissue in the liver caused by Entamoeba histolytica. Diagnosis is clinical plus imaging, serology and aspirate microscopy.

Positive in >90% of cases; rules out bacterial abscess.
Shows ‘anchovy sauce’ pus; sterile culture; confirms diagnosis when serology is equivocal.
Used when ultrasound is inconclusive; shows rim‑enhancing lesion.

sections.p: Severity is graded by size, number of lesions and presence of complications such as rupture or sepsis.

sections.p: Patients have high‑grade fever, chills, right upper quadrant pain and tender hepatomegaly. Jaundice is uncommon unless the abscess ruptures into biliary tree.
Investigations focus on confirming the diagnosis and ruling out bacterial abscess.
Rupture into pleural space, peritoneum or biliary tree, sepsis, and hepatic failure are life‑threatening.
Treat with metronidazole, supportive care, and drainage if indicated.

faq.q: Why is metronidazole preferred over tinidazole?
faq.a: Metronidazole penetrates abscess cavity better and is widely available in low‑resource settings.

faq.q: Can a patient with amoebic abscess be discharged after 48 hours?
faq.a: Only if afebrile, pain controlled, and imaging shows stable lesion; otherwise continue inpatient monitoring.

faq.q: What if the patient has a penicillin allergy?
faq.a: Metronidazole is not a beta‑lactam; allergy does not affect its use.

exam: What is the first investigation you would order in a patient with RUQ pain and fever? — Ultrasound to detect a hypoechoic lesion and guide aspiration.

How would you differentiate an amoebic abscess from a pyogenic one clinically? — Amoebic abscess is usually solitary, sterile on culture, and serology positive; pyogenic is often multiloculated and culture positive.
What is the most common complication that can be life‑threatening? — Rupture into the pleural cavity causing haemothorax or into the peritoneum causing peritonitis.
Why is metronidazole chosen over clindamycin? — Metronidazole has better abscess penetration and is effective against E. histolytica; clindamycin has higher resistance and toxicity.
When is percutaneous drainage indicated? — Lesions >5 cm, multiloculated, or not responding to medical therapy after 48–72 hours.
What red flag would prompt immediate surgical consultation? — Sudden haemodynamic instability or evidence of rupture into the pleural cavity on imaging.
